title: Delivery model, gates and review
summary:
This part settles how work reaches `dev`, `pre-prod` and `prod` after the lockdown: branches and merge authority, the fast gate every change passes before it merges into `dev`, the release run and its step list, test tiers, visual regression and screenshot evidence, batches and the packet you review before each `prod` merge, the rewrite phase and legacy hotfixes, enforcement without GitHub protection, hosted CI, deployments, parallel agents, Linear, where the lockdown lives, and rollback. Budgets and tier durations are part 07's (P-GATE-SCOPE, P-TEST-TIERS); the repository, live hosts, releases and open PRs are decided in parts 01, 03 and 08, and cards here point there instead of repeating them.

DEL-01 lists the facts the model is built on, checked on 2026-10-21 and 2026-10-22: GitHub Free cannot protect a branch or auto-merge in this private repository; `gh` on Claw Mini is signed in to three GitHub accounts: Daniel's, a second personal account and a work account, each with repo and workflow scopes, so agents act as your account and can also use the other two; no hosted CI job has started since 2026-10-13; and a full local pass takes about 20 minutes on Claw Mini.

The decisions that matter most:

- DEL-81 (your answer of 27 Oct, with its amendments) over DEL-02 to DEL-04 and DEL-63: three branches. `main` was renamed `prod`, today's `dev` was renamed `pre-prod` and a new `dev` is the default branch. Development agents (Sonnet) work in parallel and merge into `dev` after the fast gate, unit tests only and ideally under five seconds. The release agent merges batches of up to 20 into `pre-prod` and runs the long suites for what each batch affects, fixing forward. `prod` holds what you have reviewed and moves only when an agent merges a frozen candidate cut from `pre-prod` on your go; the checker and the adversarial reviews run on Opus, at most two Opus agents at once. A deploy is a separate go (DEL-40), so richview.ai keeps the legacy site until you choose the first rewrite deploy, while `dev` deploys a preview behind a Cloudflare Access sign-in you hold.
- DEL-06 (your answers of 26 and 27 Oct): ideas outside the lockdown merge into `dev` as declared feature or design PRs without pinging you, website changes included; going public stays on your go. They reach you as cards from a separate feature and design log, and rejected and deferred ones are reverted before the `prod` merge.
- DEL-08: the gate commands (`rv-gate fast`, `release`, `full` and `prod candidate/<n>`) and the step registry that says which step runs in which. Measured steps take about 15 minutes for a code-changing batch, paid once per release run, before about a dozen steps other parts route here that are not built yet.
- DEL-24, DEL-25 and DEL-50: the fast tier takes 9.7–13.7 s warm but 36.6–61.3 s after an edit, so it misses your 30 s maximum and DEL-81's five-second target until the measured waste is removed and impact tracing narrows what runs; Lenovo, which your rule names, has not been measured.
- DEL-28, DEL-29 and DEL-64: an exact pixel diff of each release run against the previous `pre-prod` head; the `prod` baseline moves only with the `prod` merge on your go, and during the rewrite design cards come per component and style, not per PR.
- DEL-32, DEL-34 and DEL-36: each PR declares `none`, `design` or `feature`; your packet holds the design and feature cards plus a deploy card; tests may be deleted with a reason and gate steps are not removed by an agent (DEL-68), which DEL-81's "anything that slows development can change" leaves open for you.
- DEL-37 (your answer, then DEL-81): enforcement is a committed pre-push hook that refuses `prod`, `pre-prod`, `main` and `candidate/*` from agent checkouts, plus the audit (DEL-38). There is no gate macOS user and no deny list, and agents have all the access.

Needs your explicit authorization: every `prod` merge, changing origin settings (default branch, protection, auto-merge, Actions, workflows), every deploy, every rollback outside the pre-authorized one in DEL-48, legacy fixes (there is no legacy hotfix), deleting tags or releases, and any spending. Agents delete branches and set up automations, such as the evidence backup, without asking. DEL-05 draws the full line.

How to answer: **accept** keeps the proposal as written (where options are listed, the proposal is the recommended option); **edit** replaces it with your text; **reject** drops it from the rewrite; **defer** leaves it open. Observed cards were measured or checked for this part on Claw Mini at `b4db233`; stated cards rest on briefs, tickets or docs not re-checked here; inferred cards are proposals built from that evidence, and a step whose command does not exist yet says “not built” and “not measured”. Part 08's cross-part contradiction cards (OPN-50 to OPN-68) decide conflicts involving this part's cards and should be answered first.

items.title: Branch names and the default branch
items.question: Which long-lived branches exist, what does each hold, which one is the default, and where do `dev` and `prod` start?
items.why: Agents start worktrees and PRs from the default branch, so it decides where work lands. Parts 01 and 08 keep today's `main` as the pre-rewrite reference (D-REPO-SPLIT, D-PROD-BASELINE) and leave the branch mechanics to this card. A from-scratch rewrite also forces a choice: either `prod` equals the live site, and an unfinished rewrite goes public at the first batch, or `prod` holds what you have reviewed and the live site follows only on a separate go.
items.proposed: `prod` holds what Daniel has reviewed and accepted, and it is the only branch the rewrite deploys from; a deploy is a separate go (DEL-40), so `prod` can run ahead of the live site, and richview.ai keeps serving the legacy baseline until Daniel authorizes the first rewrite deploy. `dev` is the default branch, from which every worktree and PR starts. Both are created from the pre-rewrite baseline once part 08's changes to `main` are done, the legacy hotfix included (D-PROD-BASELINE, D-LEGACY-FREEZE). `main` stays frozen at that baseline as the legacy reference (D-REPO-SPLIT): it receives only legacy hotfixes Daniel authorizes (DEL-65), and the pre-push hook rejects every other push to it (DEL-37). Task branches are named `<kind>/s27-<n>-<slug>` and deleted after merge; frozen candidates are `candidate/<n>` (DEL-63). `publish/news` and the PR #70 branch stay outside this model: the RichView News session improves News there now and deploys on Daniel's go (D-NEWS-LIVE, INT-74). Creating `prod` and `dev` and changing the default branch need Daniel's explicit authorization.

items.title: The gate commands: fast, release and full
items.question: What does each gate command run, who runs it and when, and what does it cost?
items.why: DEL-81 replaced the one gate that every merge passed with three tiers: a fast gate before each push to `dev`, a release run for each `pre-prod` batch and a full run for the candidate. One registry still has to list every step once, so that none runs twice and none is forgotten. Part 08 (D-HARNESS-PR68) leaves the single required list to this card, other parts route about a dozen checks to it, and part 07 cites it as DEL-08.
items.proposed:
Daniel's DEL-81 answer supersedes the earlier proposal that every change passes this gate into `dev`. `rv-gate` has four commands (AGENTS.md): `rv-gate fast` before every push to `dev`; `rv-gate release`, which the release agent runs per batch of up to 20 merges, merging `dev` into `pre-prod` and running the long suites for what the batch affects; `rv-gate full` on `pre-prod` before a candidate; and `rv-gate prod candidate/<n>` on each frozen candidate (DEL-33, DEL-71). `rv-gate steps` lists every step with its tier and cards, and a step that is not built yet reports `unrun` with its reason until it exists.

The fast gate is unit tests only, ideally under five seconds. It runs the unit tests of the changed crates and of the crates that `include_str!` a changed file, `cargo clippy -D warnings` of them and their dependents, the node tests of the tools whose folder changed and rustfmt on the changed files; impact tracing selects what a change can affect. No commit, pre-push or stop hook beyond DEL-37's push block slows development, and an agent runs browser, visual or end-to-end checks in `dev` when it judges them useful.

The release run runs the rest of this registry on `pre-prod`'s combined state, for what the batch affects, from the gate code of the previous release, so that a batch cannot loosen the check that judges it (DEL-36), and the release agent fixes forward until it passes. Only release and candidate receipts are evidence (DEL-20, DEL-21). This registry is the single list of steps, with where each runs:

items.title: Data integrity
items.question: Which existing suites prove that a report’s data stays traceable and exact where readers inspect it, and run in the release run?
items.why: INT-11 does not maximize fidelity; it guarantees that a story stays traceable and editable, and leaves presentation choices such as smoothed curves to the author. This check keeps the data side of that guarantee: every value a reader sees equals the source at the precision the author chose (Daniel's FEA-CH-37 answer), RichView never fabricates rows, and no bug silently corrupts a value. Six browser suites check exactness today. `verify-bar-paint` (DEL-15) also renders one report of two four-bar charts in all five builtin styles at 1440 and 420 px and checks the exact source values in accessible names and keyboard readouts, and the authoring proof compares content and data across three styles (DEL-17); a check over every example and style is DEL-52.
items.proposed: The release run runs the data-integrity suites `node scripts/verify-<suite>.mjs` for numeric-safety, numeric-zoom, source-tables, temporal-fidelity, temporal-decimals and csv-decimals (79.1 s together, all passing), alongside the cross-style value check (DEL-52). They guard what INT-11 and Daniel's FEA-CH-37 answer keep: every value a reader sees in labels, readouts, Table, CSV and exports equals the source at the author's chosen precision (the three-digit default, or the precision set per chart or element) and never shows more (DEL-80); no fabricated, dropped or altered rows; and no bug that silently corrupts data, such as lost decimals, shifted dates, overflow at the extremes or values that change under zoom or export. Visual transformations the author chooses, such as smoothed curves (FEA-CH-03), are allowed and are not checked against literal precision; the values behind them stay in the readouts and data views at the author's precision. Suites that assert every source digit today (`csv-decimals`, `temporal-decimals`, `source-tables`) change to assert the author's precision instead. Proves: values, units, calendars and extremes survive interaction, tables, CSV downloads and export in Chromium. Misses: most of these suites render one style at one desktop width, so other styles and phone widths are DEL-52’s; readouts taken during an animation; a chart or figure without a source note, which `richview check` warns about (FEA-RP-09) but no suite fails on; and data the fixtures do not contain.

items.title: Gate receipts
items.question: What record does every gate run leave, and where?
items.why: Merging without review replaces your look at each PR with evidence; the evidence must say exactly what was tested and what was not.
items.proposed: Every release run and every candidate run writes a receipt into the evidence store (DEL-61) on Claw Mini, outside any worktree; a fast-gate run leaves only its output, which is not evidence (DEL-21, DEL-81). A receipt holds commit and tree hashes; toolchain, browser and macOS build versions; the build manifest's artifact hashes; each step's command, result, duration and log path; unrun steps with reasons; and the screenshot manifest. The `pre-prod` merge commit names the release receipt's ID, and the release summary lists the merges the batch covered. A red step stays red until a new run passes; receipts are never edited and are kept for the life of the repository. Logs and run folders are not: the store keeps the run folder only for each open PR's latest run and the latest full and prod runs, so a merged PR's logs go with its run folder while its receipt, with the log paths it recorded, stays.

items.why: Progress was repeatedly reported ahead of evidence: review states read as passed gates, builds as completion, partial work as parity. Part 01's G-HONEST-CLAIMS leaves honest progress reporting to this part.

items.title: Deliberate-mutation check
items.question: How is the fast tier shown to still catch real breakage, and when is that repeated?
items.why: A fast number is worthless if the tier no longer fails when the code is wrong; your tier standard requires this check.
items.proposed:
When the rewrite's tiers are first set, after each test audit (DEL-36) and whenever the gate changes, an agent makes one deliberate mutation per core behaviour in an isolated copy, never a shared worktree, records which tier catches it and restores the source byte for byte. A behaviour that only a slower tier catches gets a fast representative or a named exception in DELIVERY.md. Core behaviours: parsing and schema errors, style cascade, chart scales and geometry, number and date formatting, output bounds, data resolution, immutable publish storage and MCP contracts. The run on `b4db233` for this part mutated four sites:

| Mutation | fast (436) | `--lib` (190) | slow (2) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M1: output limit removed, `crates/richview-core/src/lib.rs:56` | survives | survives | caught |
| M2: resume re-sends journaled parts, `crates/richview-app/src/asset_upload/upload.rs:567` | survives | caught, by the slow test it contains | caught |
| M3: pie `<0.1%` label removed, `richview-chart/src/rmd_render.rs:3208` | caught | survives | — |
| M4: header-data error removed, `crates/richview-core/src/parser.rs:264-266` | survives | survives | — |

It covered three of the eight behaviours (output bounds, number formatting, parsing errors) plus upload resume; style cascade, scales and geometry, date formatting, data resolution, publish storage and MCP contracts were not mutated. M4 survives every tier because `crates/richview-core/src/folder.rs:203-206` adds the same error again during rendering, so no test tells the two checks apart; it needs a fast parser test that asserts the header-data error without rendering. The tiers count as accepted only after a full run with one mutation per behaviour, repeated once DEL-25's representatives exist. Deleting a test needs no mutation proof (Daniel's DEL-68 answer); this run is what shows that, after deletions and tier moves, every core behaviour is still caught at the fast tier. items.title: Diff method and threshold
items.question: How are captures compared between builds, and how much difference passes?
items.why: A tolerance lets small regressions through, and an exact threshold works only if captures are deterministic. They are: two captures of the same build, about 50 minutes apart under load, produced 1,200 byte-identical captures.
items.proposed: Each capture is compared with the same capture of the previous `pre-prod` head, the last release. Identical SHA-256 bytes pass; otherwise the gate decodes both images, counts changed pixels and writes a diff overlay and a side-by-side image. The threshold is exact: zero changed pixels unless the PR declares a visual change (DEL-32). Baselines are valid only for the same host, macOS build, browser build, GPU path for WebGL (hardware, or SwiftShader by flag), fonts and Playwright version; an upgrade, an OS update included, is its own PR that shows identical captures or declares the change (DEL-49). Nondeterminism is fixed at its cause, never absorbed by a tolerance.

options.label: Small tolerance, such as 0.1 % of pixels

items.question: Which merged changes reach you as decisions, and how is that classification enforced?
items.why: You review only design-quality and feature decisions. If agents classify freely, a visual or scope change can pass as a fix; if every implementation of an accepted item counts as a feature, nearly every rewrite PR becomes a card.
items.proposed: Every PR declares `decision: none`, `design` or `feature` and names the lockdown items it implements. `feature`: the PR changes scope: it adds or changes a public surface, component, type, style or behaviour that no accepted item specifies, or changes or removes what an accepted item specifies (DEL-06). Removing legacy behaviour that no accepted item specifies is not a feature decision: INT-49 drops it, the PR names INT-49, and the packet appendix lists the removal. `design`: a capture differs from the `prod` baseline, or tokens, typography, motion or public copy change. `none`: everything else, including fixes that restore the `prod` look and implementations of accepted items that change no capture. Implementing an accepted item as written is not a feature decision: the packet appendix lists it with its evidence, and any visual difference makes it a design card. The release run enforces the class: it flags a merge declared `none` when a changed capture differs from the `prod` baseline, and a public-surface snapshot change (DEL-53) unless its PR declared `feature` or named the accepted items that specify it; the release agent fixes forward by reclassifying or reverting. While `prod` still holds legacy output, nearly every rendering PR is `design`; those cards are batched per component and style, not per PR (DEL-64). A PR that changes the website merges into `dev` like any other change and needs no grant (Daniel's DEL-06 answer, amended 2026-10-27); only going public waits for his go.

items.title: Batches and the frozen prod candidate
items.question: What is a batch, who closes it, and which exact commit do the packet and the `prod` merge describe?
items.why: DEL-04 requires `prod`'s tree to equal a gated tree, but `pre-prod` keeps receiving release batches while you review and while agents revert rejected cards; a `pre-prod` to `prod` merge would take whatever `pre-prod` is at that moment. Nothing defined a packet batch or who closes it, and DEL-81 added release batches, which are a different thing.
items.proposed: Two kinds of batch exist. A release batch is the release agent's: up to 20 merges taken from `dev` into `pre-prod` and run through the release run (DEL-81, DEL-08). A packet batch is a Linear milestone in the RichView project: the chief of staff closes it when its issues are merged or deferred and no regression is open against `pre-prod`, or when Daniel asks for a packet. Closing it runs the full run on `pre-prod` and cuts a frozen candidate branch, `candidate/<n>`, from the `pre-prod` head; `rv-gate prod candidate/<n>` runs on it, the packet describes it, and `prod` moves from it by `rv-gate merge-prod` on Daniel's go (DEL-04). The candidate is a frozen state of `pre-prod`, never the moving head, so `prod` still receives only what came through `dev` and `pre-prod` (DEL-02, DEL-81). `dev` and `pre-prod` keep moving meanwhile, and later work waits for the next packet batch. The reverts that Daniel's answers require are made on the candidate and, through ordinary reverts, on `pre-prod` and `dev`; the candidate reruns `rv-gate prod` before the merge. Only the gate writes candidate branches.

items.title: Review agents advise; they do not gate
items.question: Do independent review agents gate merges into `dev`?
items.why: Earlier RichView briefs required independent adversarial design critiques, your general rule avoids mandatory reviewer agents, and review verdicts are not deterministic.
items.proposed: Review agents are required steps, not optional sensors (Daniel's DEL-68 answer), and an agent can judge design quality (INT-67). An adversarial review, run by an Opus agent, reads each release batch on `pre-prod` before its candidate is frozen (DEL-81). The checker and the adversarial reviews run on Opus, and at most two Opus agents run at once across the build (DEL-81). items.title: Changes that weaken the gate
items.question: May agents merge changes that loosen the gate itself without asking?
items.why: Agents under pressure edit or skip tests to make them pass; a gate that the same PR can loosen protects nothing. Your brief limits your review to design and feature decisions, so the protection should be automatic wherever a proof exists.
items.proposed:
Tests are not sacred; the process is (Daniel's DEL-68 answer). Adding checks merges freely. Agents may delete a test without asking when it is no longer needed: unit tests at will, end-to-end tests whose feature was removed or no longer makes sense, and tests a test audit finds merely formal, testing the obvious or repeating another test. A test audit runs when an agent or Daniel asks for one. A skipped test counts as deleted, and moving a test to a slower tier is an ordinary change. No mutation proof is needed: each deleted test is listed with its reason in the dev change log (DEL-70) and the before-and-after report (DEL-69), and DEL-26's mutation run after each audit shows that every core behaviour is still caught.

An agent can never remove or skip a step of the process: a step of the fast gate or the release run (DEL-08), the prod tests (DEL-71), a capture step (DEL-27) or a required review (DEL-35). Elements inside a step may change; adding or removing a step is Daniel's decision, except where DEL-81 (later) lets steps change because they slow development (see conflicts). Three kinds of change still come to him as cards, because they loosen a check without deleting a test: raising a threshold, budget or baseline (part 07 routes these to him already, P-REGRESSION-GATE; DEL-81 lets thresholds that slow development change, and which thresholds still come to him is open); changing the detector that finds removed steps and raised thresholds; and changing `docs/lockdown/answers/` other than through DEL-66. The release run and its detector run from the gate code of the previous release, never from the batch's own, so a PR cannot loosen the check that judges it. During the rewrite, legacy tests retire through DEL-64's retirement list, which gives each test's reason.

items.title: Enforcement without GitHub branch protection
items.question: How are “only through the gate” and “`prod` moves only on Daniel's go” enforced when GitHub cannot do it?
items.why: On GitHub Free a private repository gets no protection, rulesets or auto-merge, every collaborator can push to any branch, merge PRs and create releases, and agents hold your credentials. Without a mechanism the model rests on instructions, which Claude Code treats as context, not enforcement.
items.proposed: Enforcement is local, and detection does not depend on GitHub identities. The gate runs as its own macOS user on Claw Mini: only that user can write the gate checkout, the gate code, the receipts and the evidence store (DEL-61), so no agent can fake a receipt, and it pushes the squash commit to `dev` itself. In agent checkouts a repository pre-push hook rejects pushes to `prod`, `dev` and candidate branches (DEL-02 leaves no frozen `main`), and agent tool settings (Claude Code permissions with a PreToolUse policy hook, and Codex's equivalent) deny `--no-verify`, force pushes other than `--force-with-lease` on the agent's own task branch, `gh pr merge`, GitHub API writes, `wrangler` (including through `npx`), `curl` with a write method, and deploy, release and publish commands. Agents still push task branches with a write token, which GitHub Free cannot limit per branch, so the audit (DEL-38) is the backstop: a `dev` commit without a gate receipt, or a `prod` move without Daniel's recorded go, is an incident. The merge into `prod` is the one command an agent runs on Daniel's go once the prod-candidate gate passes (DEL-04); how that command proves his go to the hook, the agent settings and the audit is open. Before the gate starts, the tokens of accounts other than the agents' own leave the agents' environment: `gh` on Claw Mini holds signed-in tokens for three GitHub accounts: Daniel's, a second personal account and a work account, each with repo and workflow scopes, so today any agent can act as any of them. No collaborator is invited (OPN-24), so every writer today is Daniel or an agent; if DEL-04's named collaborators are added later, their own checkouts have no hooks, and for them the rule is social, backed by the audit.

items.title: Worktrees and isolation
items.question: How do parallel agents stay out of each other's way?
items.why: Agents collided in October: a shared Cargo target ran a builder from another worktree, and five pairs of open PRs conflict (DEL-81 now runs many agents in parallel, so isolation matters more): #63 with #67, #64 with #66, #64 with #70, #65 with #69 and #67 with #69.
items.proposed:
One task is one Linear issue, one worktree under `.claude/worktrees/<slug>` from fresh `origin/dev`, one branch and one PR. Development agents run in parallel, as many as there are fully independent pieces of work, on Sonnet with their subagents; the lockdown session splits the work into independent streams and briefs them (Daniel's DEL-81 answer). Agents never edit another task's worktree or the primary checkout. They record in the issue which modules they will change, and overlapping claims are sequenced. On Claw Mini every stream and subagent builds in the one shared Cargo target, one build at a time under its lock, with a stamping wrapper so that the target never builds another checkout's sources and a disk floor of 10 GiB (Daniel, 2026-10-29; it was 40) (DEL-22, AGENTS.md). Edit-loop results are not evidence; only release and candidate receipts are. The owner deletes its worktree and branch after the merge; nobody deletes another task's worktree or shared caches.

**Owned paths, ledger and mailbox** (Daniel, 29 Oct 2026, relayed by the chief of staff; waiting for his confirmation in the app). The organizer, the release agent, keeps an OWNERS map per path; an agent changes only paths it owns or was granted. A shared ledger and one mailbox per agent replace routine messages: agents read them at seams, before starting a packet and before pushing, and reconcile with what else landed only as far as their packet needs. Direct messages are kept for three cases: your commit broke `dev`, you are blocking someone now, or Daniel's ruling changes work in flight. Work comes in packets of 3 to 6 hours with one owner each, and there is no fixed cap on the number of streams.

Trust is set per kind of change, and earned:

| Change | Evidence that is enough | Where you see it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `none`: fixes, refactors, accepted items implemented with no capture change (DEL-32) | A passing dev-gate receipt; a mutation proof for any weakened test (DEL-36) | Packet appendix only, plus the sample below |

items.title: Fast parallel development: dev, pre-prod and a release agent
items.question: How does development run fast: who merges where, which tests run when, and how do many agents work at once?
items.why: After 22 hours the rewrite had 23 merges and 21% of lockdown items checked. Every change went through the full gate alone, behind a lock, with hooks and reviews, and the agent spent much of its time waiting. Daniel wants a massive speed-up across the whole system.
items.proposed:
Three branches. Today's `dev` is renamed `pre-prod`; a new `dev` is created from it and becomes the default branch; `prod` moves only on Daniel's go.

- **Development agents** run in parallel, as many as there are fully independent pieces of work, each in its own worktree. They merge into `dev` freely. No commit, pre-push or stop hooks slow them down.
- **Testing in `dev` is at the agent's discretion.** The fast gate is unit tests only, ideally under five seconds. Agents run browser, visual or end-to-end checks when they judge it useful, for example to see a new chart.
- **Impact tracing.** Dependencies between crates, modules and suites are traced automatically, so the fast gate and the release run only the tests a change can affect; tests that cannot be affected are not run.
- **The release agent** merges `dev` into `pre-prod` after a batch of changes (three, five or ten, by their size and significance). It runs the long-running suites (end-to-end, browsers, visual, data integrity, PDF) on the combined state, for what the batch affects, and fixes forward until everything works together.
- **`prod`** is cut from `pre-prod` on Daniel's go, after the full run (DEL-04, DEL-71 apply to that step).
- **The lockdown session leads:** it splits the work into independent streams, briefs the agents, and relays Daniel.

items.title: The geometry model is the chart test oracle
items.question: Do chart, value, interaction and motion checks read the engine's geometry model through one named interface, with a check that the canvas really draws that model, and does ARC-08's contract test join the release run?

items.title: Motion tests for WebGL animation
items.question: How are chart and report animations tested automatically, now that entrances are drawn WebGL frames rather than CSS animations?
items.why: Your INT-17 answer makes rich animation part of the craft that decides whether RichView succeeds, and your INT-12 answer sets its direction: delightful and smooth, “the whimsical quality of Studio Ghibli meets the polish of Apple's website animations”. Today's motion checks (DEL-15's `bar-paint` and `motion-runtime`, DEL-30) read CSS animations on chart SVG and are reported unrun under WebGL, so motion could only be judged by eye.
items.proposed:
Every motion is specified as data in the engine: what moves, duration, curve and stagger (FEA-CH-51, FEA-CH-52, FEA-RP-35). The runtime's animation clock can be paused and stepped by tools through `window.__richview` (TYP-97), like `settled()`.

The motion suite steps each transition to fixed fractions (0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 %) and asserts on the geometry model (DEL-72) at each: bars stay on their baseline; axes, titles and legends do not move; marks move monotonically towards their target; a readout taken mid-frame shows the target value at the author's precision, never an interpolated one; an entrance runs once and never replays on scroll-back or repaint; the last frame equals the settled frame; reduced motion shows the settled frame from the first frame (FEA-RP-36).

Frames captured at those fractions on the pinned capture path (DEL-73) are diffed exactly, like stills, in every release run whose batch changes a capture, and feed the before-and-after report (DEL-69). Real-speed clips on the GPU path go to the report, where a review agent on the model you use at the time judges them against INT-12's direction (DEL-35, Daniel's DEL-68 answer) and you can adjust. Pacing stays PRF-21 and PRF-27. The suite covers chart entrances and transitions, scrollytelling steps (FEA-RP-48), the style switch (STY-43), the landing (FEA-BR-21) and any motion INT-17's and INT-12's richer animation adds.

items.title: The fresh-agent run: harness and schedule
items.question: How, how often and with which agents does INT-69's fresh-agent test run?
items.why: INT-69 sets the bar, and Daniel's INT-21 answer makes agent use a headline bet and its measurement a feature (FEA-SF-65), but no harness, schedule, agent products or datasets exist, so whether a new agent succeeds is known only by trying it yourself.
items.proposed: The harness, which is the measurement feature of FEA-SF-65 run as a gate, starts Claude Code and Codex, each in an empty sandbox outside any checkout, with only the candidate's installed CLI and MCP server and a network limited to the model API. Each gets a fixed brief and one of several rotating real tasks and datasets, and its transcript, tool calls, attempts and final report are recorded. Each run is scored against INT-69's bar: a sourced report with prose, at least three chart types (one of them from a family added since the last run) and a table, no error diagnostics, and a clean `check` by the second attempt without reading RichView's source; the score also records the attempts, the errors hit and the tool calls, so that it can be tracked over time. Agents are not deterministic, so the result is a pass rate over three runs per product. It runs at each candidate and weekly on the `pre-prod` head, where DEL-81 runs the long suites; the scores are kept as a series, the packet appendix shows pass rates, the trend and the diagnostics that confused agents, and each confusion caused by docs or diagnostics becomes an issue, so that RichView is changed until agents understand it as easily as possible (Daniel's INT-21 answer). items.title: Values at the author's precision, and nothing more precise
items.question: Your FEA-CH-37 answer says readers never get more precision than the author chose. What does the gate check, and what counts as retrievable?
items.why: DEL-16 and DEL-52 were written to prove the opposite: exact source values in readouts, Table and CSV. They have to be rewritten, and a new check must prove that the exact values are absent.
items.proposed:
DEL-16 and DEL-52 assert that every value a reader sees (labels, readouts, Table, CSV, accessible names, downloads, PDF text) equals the source rounded by the author's precision rule (the three-digit default, or the precision set per chart or element), identical across styles and widths.

A disclosure check then scans every output (the HTML, embedded data, the runtime's model interface (DEL-72), CSV, downloads and PDF) of fixtures whose source carries more digits than shown, and fails when any value appears with more precision than its element allows.

Open: whether mark coordinates count. A second open point: whether the raw source (`/raw/...`, TYP-65's `source`) and the stored record count. Daniel's INT-03 answer has the rendered page travel with its source, and his FEA-CH-37 answer says readers cannot retrieve more precision than the author chose. Options: serve raw source and the stored record only to roles that may edit the story, so a reader gets the page, not the source; or serve the source to every reader and treat its digits as the author's choice of what to publish, with the disclosure check scanning it. Positions drawn from exact values let a determined reader recover more digits than shown; quantizing positions to the shown precision can move marks visibly. Options below.

options.detail: No value with more digits in any output; coordinates stay exact, so close reading of the drawing can recover more precision.

options.label: Also quantize coordinates
options.detail: Nothing recoverable; marks plotted from rounded values can shift by up to the rounding step.

items.title: Pre-launch gate phase
items.question: During pre-launch, may the gate rerun a failed step once and rotate proven slow checks while preserving visible evidence?
items.why: Daniel prioritised a full gate below ten minutes on 30 October 2026 and explicitly allowed reruns and measured test reduction during pre-launch. The strict launch gate remains available through one recorded phase switch.
items.proposed:
tools/rv-gate/phase.json records phase (prelaunch or launch), since and by. Daniel decides when launch begins. Every receipt records its frozen phase and policy. In prelaunch, every tier, including prod, reruns a failed step once in a fresh process and fresh browser. A successful rerun passes with flaky=true; both attempts, failures, logs and raw artifacts remain visible. Two failures stay failed, and cancellation is not a new attempt. In launch the first failed step stays failed.

The value ledger counts actual full/prod step executions, final pass/fail, failures recovered on rerun, sole failures and conditional failures such as webkit given chromium-pass. It reports actual execution cost separately from queue time, with timing provenance; parallel receipt duration cannot substitute for execution time, and missing timing remains unknown.

Only a lead-approved list in phase.json may rotate. An eligible step has no failure, including a failed first attempt, in at least its latest 20 full/prod executions and a measured median execution time of at least 200 seconds. Artifact dependencies such as build and captures and cheap steps under 60 seconds always run. Each full selects a deterministic third, and each rotated step runs at least every third full, including after list changes. Other rotated steps remain visible as unrun with reason prelaunch rotation and a frozen plan; only those explicit planned gaps may authorize pre-prod promotion. Prod runs all steps, with the one prelaunch rerun. Switching to launch restores the strict full cohort and first-attempt verdict.

Daniel’s dated personal-quota exception pauses only fresh-agent in prelaunch full runs until 2026-10-31T18:00:00.581308Z (31 October 19:00 Prague). It never switches to the work account. The exact expiry and reason are frozen in policy and result; prod and launch remain complete. At expiry fresh-agent runs again and new promotion refuses a skipped result. Historical audits use the frozen valid policy and execution time.

rv-gate value [--since YYYY-MM-DD] writes evidence/value.json and a Markdown table. Recommendations never retire a check automatically; the lead approves rotation changes and Daniel decides retirement. The reviewer reads the ledger per batch and maintains QUALITY.md. Existing budget/oracle/precision/safety rules remain. The first measured full after adoption reports actual wall time and receipt identity; estimates do not prove the ten-minute target.
